title: Mandelson tried to arrange ‘under radar’ meeting involving ex-lobbying colleague and Trump adviser, documents reveal – UK politics live
description:
The disgraced peer said he wanted to hold a lunch to discuss ‘alternative options’ to the World Trade Organization

The Liberal Democrats are saying the UK needs a proper plan for immigration. This is from the party’s asylum and immigration spokesperson, Paul Kohler.

Britain needs to regain control of its immigration system after the chaos of Brexit. Yet sixteen years after David Cameron’s ‘tens of thousands’ pledge, six prime ministers and ten home secretaries have overseen wild swings in immigration numbers with net migration now set to fall below zero.

Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services.

The fall in net migration is mainly a result of changes made by the previous Conservative government. We now need to go even further with a legally binding annual cap, set by parliament, at a far lower level.

text: How Mandelson as ambassador sought to arrange 'under radar' meeting involving ex-lobbying colleague and Trump adviser
Henry Dyer is a Guardian investigations correspondent.

Peter Mandelson sought to organise an “under the radar” meeting in Washington with an economic adviser to Donald Trump and a member of his former lobbying firm, Global Counsel. He did so while ambassador in April 2025 and still holding his shares in Global Counsel.
Mandelson wanted to hold a lunch to discuss “alternative options” to the World Trade Organization and on how “likeminded partners come to terms with China and its practices”.
After discussing dates with American counterparts, he forwarded the emails to a Global Counsel employee. He asked: “Do you have date preference for trade think in?”
Tories accuses Mandelson of 'staggering arrogance', after ex-ambassador publishes article with Brexit advice for PM
In the Commons, Charlie Dewhirst, a shadow minister, replied to Dan Jarvis on behalf of the Conservative party. Here are the main points he made.
He criticised the fact that Mandelson was allowed to keep his shareholding in Global Counsel. He said:

double quotation markOn 11 March [Darren Jones, the then Cabinet Office minister] told this house that the rules required new civil servants to give up such interests before taking office. Seemingly not this one.

Dewhirst said that in March MPs the foreign secetary was told a sale of the shares had been agreed. That was not right, he said. And he said, when a correction was issued, Mandelson was invited to review it first.
Dewhirst said he was surprised that only one message sent via Signal has been disclosed.
He asked Jarvis to give details about what documents the police wanted the government to hold back.
He accused Mandelson of “staggering arrogance”, referring to an article Mandelson has published on Unherd today advising the PM on EU policy.

double quotation markAnd by the way, where is Mr. Mandelson this morning? In print, lecturing the prime minister about how to negotiate with Brussels. No apology, no humility, just more advice. It is staggering arrogance. So will the minister confirm that nobody in this government is taking his advice?
In response, Jarvis said that only a “small number” of documents were still being held back. He said he would not give further details about them.
And he gave Dewhirst a “catagorical assurance” that the government would not be taking advice from Mandelson.
In his article, Mandelson said:

double quotation markIf the government decides that fundamentally changing the UK-EU relationship is desirable and viable, it requires the permission of the British people to do so at the next general election. Prefacing this with informal brainstorming with the EU is a good idea because it will clarify the options available. The public’s definitive verdict would then await a post-negotiation referendum, as Burnham has now clarified. Throughout, the prime minister in particular, but also the foreign secretary, chancellor and other ministers, will need to demonstrate considerable conviction and persuasiveness about why we need to roll back Brexit. The EU will want to know that the government’s heart really is in a new beginning and that it can secure clear public backing for it.
Jarvis said the government has already tightened procedures relating to ministerial appointments in the light of the way the appointment of Mandelson as an ambassador backfired.

double quotation markThe government has already taken action by strengthening the arrangements governing direct ministerial appointments, including more rigorous due diligence and clearer responsibilities for identifying and managing risks, and in developing a strengthened policy around the management of the conflict of interests. The FCDO has also confirmed that future diplomatic appointments will not be made or announced before the necessary security clearance has been granted, and is strengthening the arrangements for scrutinising political appointments to senior diplomatic posts, including through a role for the foreign affairs select committee.
He said Sir Adrian Fulford’s review of vetting procedures was nearing completion.
And he ended, as he started his statement, by stressing the importance of remembering Jeffrey Epstein’s victims.
Security minister Dan Jarvis says some Mandelson documents still being withheld at request of police
Jarvis said some documents were still being withheld at the request of the police. He said:

double quotation markA number of further documents remain withheld at the request of the Metropolitan police to avoid prejudicing their ongoing investigation. Those remaining documents will be published once the police confirm that doing so will not risk prejudicing their investigation or any subsequent legal processes.
Jarvis tells MPs the documents out today also include messages sent “through non-corporate channels” (like WhatsApp).
He says this issue is already being reviewed by Sir Anthony Finkelstein, a former government chief scientific adviser for national security. This review will report in January, he says.
Minister tells MPs government's outside interests policy to be beefed up in light of Mandelson Global Counsel issues

In the Commons, Dan Jarvis, the security minister, is making a statement about the latest release of Mandelson documents. He says 32 new documents have been made public. These were previously held back at the request of the police, he says.
He says ministers were not involved in the decisions about which documents would be released in accordance with the humble address.

double quotation markThe documents include correspondence relating to the management of Mandelson’s conflicts of interest, including his ongoing stake in Global Counsel. They underline the importance not only of identifying potential conflicts of interest, but of ensuring that the arrangements put in place to manage them are effective and properly implemented.
double quotation markThe Cabinet Office will shortly publish a strengthened declaration and management of outside interests policy, which will apply across government.
How Mandelson decided to 'soften' language on China in speech in response to feedback from ex-Global Counsel colleague

Peter Mandelson consulted a former colleague from his Global Counsel lobbying firm before about the text of his Ditchley Park speech before he delivered it, according to emails released today. In response to the feedback, Mandelson said he would “soften” the language on China.
Here is Patrick Wintour’s report on the speech.
How Mandelson tried to influence Starmer's September 2025 reshuffle
Pippa Crerar is the Guardian’s political editor.
The files release today show Peter Mandelson trying to get involved in Keir Starmer’s reshuffle in September 2025.
In a short exchange of WhatsApps on 5 September 2025, Mandelson told Starmer’s chief of staff at the time, Morgan McSweeney, to “solve your Darren issue” – referring to Darren Jones.
Referring to the then science secretary, Mandelson wrote: “Are you taking peter Kyle away ….?”
In a second message, he said: “You should solve your Darren issue and put him at DSIT (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology).”
Around 45 minutes later, he asked where McSweeney was and added “I am in upstairs meeting room”.
Jones was not made science secretary. Instead he was made chief secretary to the PM.
Kyle was moved in the refshuffle. He became business secretary, and Liz Kendall replaced him as science secretary.

The reshuffle took place was prompted by the resignation of Angela Rayner over her tax affairs. In April this year McSweeney, who at that point had resigned, taking responsibility for the flawed decision to appoint Mandelson as ambassador to the US, told the foreign affairs select committee that Mandelson had not masterminded the reshuffle, though he confirmed he had sent unsolicited suggestions by text.
“He texted me his thoughts,” he told MPs. “I have to say that on reshuffle day I get texted a lot of thoughts from a lot of people”.

McSweeney told the committee that he hadn’t responded to any of Mandelson’s suggestions – which the release appears to confirm – but had been in touch with him at the end of the day. “I think we seized that day quite well,” the messages reveal he told him.

The former No 10 chief also told MPs he “might have” bumped into Mandelson in Downing Street that day, but he could not recall. The newly released messages show that the former ambassador told McSweeney exactly where in the building he was. It is unclear whether the two men actually met.

Peter Mandelson left his north London home within minutes of the publication of the new documents, the Press Association reports. He walked past waiting photographers and did not respond when they said hello.
How Mandelson's failure to sell his stake in lobbying firm after becoming ambassador concerned Foreign Office

Olly Robbins, the permanent secretary at the Foreign Office, was concerned that Peter Mandleson did not sell his shares in Global Counsel, the lobbying company he founded, when he was appointed ambassador, one letter in the file reveals.

It was sent in March, after Mandelson had been in post for more than a month. The Foreign Office thought the best solution to the conflict of interest this created would have been for Global Counsel to buy Mandelson out. But they refused to pay what Mandelson thought his shareholding was worth.
A few months later, as this continued to be a concern, Mandelson told colleagues in an email that Global Counsel should just “pull their fingers out and buy my shares”.
Mandelson's security vetting focused on his recent close contacts, not his 'whole life', No 10 told

Here is another email from Ian Collard. Sent to an official at No 10, it says that Mandelson’s vetting focused on his close contacts in recent years, which presumably addresses concerns about why the vetting process did not flag up the extent of the closeness to Jeffrey Epstein. This was sent in September, shortly after emails released in the US as part of the Epstein files showed that Mandelson had maintained a very close relationship with Epstein even after his first conviction for child sex offences.

I would note that the vetting system predominantly looks at one’s close contacts of recent years. It is not intended (in all areas of review at least) as a retrospective on someone’s whole life. I assume UKSV could explain this better, if required.
How security officials had concerns about Mandleson's 'overseas contacts'

Here is one document from the bundle. It is an email sent by Ian Collard, the chief property and security officer at the Foreign Office, after Peter Mandelson’s secruity vetting (DV – developed vetting) had been approved.

It shows that there were still concerns about his “overseas contacts” (ie, some of his foreign business friends), and that his accesss to the most sensitive information would depend on what was subsequently decided in relation to those.
A transcription of that second email is below:

From: Ian Collard *Sent: 30 January 2025 10:12To: Corin Robertson; JCSSubject: Personal/LPM OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE - HR - MANAGEMENT Dear Corin, *JCS (for Olly), An update. This information is provided in strictest confidence, to respect vetting confidence principles, because Corin and Olly are directly in my line management chain as Chief Security Officer. ESND have approved the DV clearance of Lord Mandelson. He was sent notification and his DV certificate by email (on Osprey) on the evening of 29 January 2025. It will be valid for five years. As part of the usual clearance process, UKSV identified some areas in his application for ESND to review: - I understand that Lord Mandelson’s private sector engagements are being managed by HRD and Legal Directorate through the conflict of interest process. - With regard to personal conduct, I understand that Lord Mandelson has received a letter from Mervyn Thomas, informing him of his responsibilities as an FCDO employee, including under the Diplomatic Service Regulations. - Matters pertaining to his overseas contacts will certainly be reviewed by the STRAP Authorities. I am unable to assure about the decision they will take. Their decision will determine the access that Lord Mandelson has to the most sensitive information and meetings. ESND shared with Lord Mandelson (and separately with *JCS in Americas Directorate) the STRAP application forms, which we have asked Lord Mandelson to complete as an urgent priority. We will seek to expedite the processing of his application as soon as the completed forms are returned to us. Best wishes,Ian *Stars mark when a word has replaced one that appears to have been redacted
Cabinet Office publishes new tranche of Mandelson documents
The Cabinet Office has now published the latest tranche of Mandelson documents.
The file runs to 88 pages.
We have already had two releases from the Mandelson files covered by the humble address.
Here is our live blog from the first release, in March.
And here is our live blog from June, when a much bigger tranche of documents was published.
Migration Observatory on what has caused fall in net migration
The Migration Observatory, a migration thinktank based at the University of Oxford, has released this statement about the reasons for the fall in net migration recorded in today’s figures. It says

double quotation markThe fall brings UK net migration below the “tens of thousands” level that was a key unfulfilled government target throughout the 2010s. The 62% fall over the past 12 months-from 204,000 on the year ending June 2025-results from lower immigration. Net migration has fallen over 90% since the peak of 944,000 in the year ending March 2023. The data now cover two full years of data since the election, and close to a full year since Labour restricted work migration in July 2025. Immigration fell by 17% over the year, driven by fewer non-EU citizens in all major categories: work (down 25%), study (down 11%), family unification (down 30%), and asylum (down 22%). This follows 2025 restrictions making care workers and several mid-skilled jobs ineligible for work visas and suspending family reunion for refugees. The government has also raised compliance requirements for universities sponsoring international students. Emigration also remained relatively high but fell by 4% (-28,000) compared to the year ending June 2025. High emigration contributes to the overall low net migration figure, but does not result directly from current government policy – most emigrants were non-citizens who previously migrated for work or study, including under the post-Brexit immigration system when immigration was unusually high. EU citizens, primarily people who arrived under free movement, also contributed to the emigration figures, with a negative net migration figure of 45,000.
Here are the figures from the ONS showing net migration figures by category – British nationals, EU+ (EU nationals, plus Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland), and non-EU+ nationals.
Security minister Dan Jarvis to address MPs about further release of Mandelson papers

The Government is expected to publish more documents on the appointment of Peter Mandelson as US ambassador shortly, with the security minister set to address MPs at about 12.30pm, the Press Association reports. PA says:

double quotation markDan Jarvis will give a statement in the Commons on the latest release of papers which cover the vetting process into Mandelson before he was sent to Washington. The disgraced peer was sacked from his position last year after more details emerged about his close links to paedophile financier Jeffrey Epstein. The scandal played a significant role in the eventual resignation of Keir Starmer, with questions raised about how much the then-prime minister knew when he made the appointment. More than 1,500 pages of documents were published earlier this year, including messages between Mandelson and cabinet ministers. However, some were withheld at the request of the Metropolitan police as part of their investigation into the former Labour minister and spin doctor. Mandelson was arrested in February on suspicion of misconduct in public office. No charges have been made. He has denied any allegations and is co-operating with police. The Met has since informed the government the documents can be published without affecting their investigation. In February, MPs voted for the papers to be released using a parliamentary mechanism known as a “humble address” and agreed that unredacted files would be first viewed by parliament’s intelligence and security committee (ISC) before being published. The latest tranche of documents have been seen by the ISC and are now expected to be put before MPs. Previous documents have shed light on messages between Mandelson and Labour cabinet ministers. Former chief secretary to the prime minister, Darren Jones, had contacted the peer to tell him he had done a “great job” on the day of his sacking. Meanwhile, work and pensions secretary Pat McFadden had complained to Lord Mandelson that Labour backbenchers were asking “who can we tax in order to pay benefits to others”. Mandelson himself was seen to describe No 10 as “beleaguered and bereft”.
Irish PM says he's confident UK and EU will resolve outstanding tuition fees issue
Jakub Krupa writes the Guardian’s Europe live blog.

Irish prime minister Micheál Martin said he was confident the EU and the EU “will be in a position to resolve the outstanding issue” of tuition fees, as he hailed the deals on sanitary and phytosanitary rules, youth mobility, and energy.
Speaking at the beginning of the European Council meeting in Brussels, Martin said that “for the young people of Britain and the young people of Europe, this is a win-win.”

double quotation markI often felt with Brexit that the young people of Britain perhaps were not consulted as strongly in terms of the implications for youth mobility. Young people love to travel, and we don’t need to be placing barriers in the way of young people accessing education, accessing work. In Europe, that should never be the case and I believe we can facilitate that.
On SPS, he said the deal was “very good news for Ireland and the UK” as it will “remove barriers” affecting small to medium size companies in particular.
The deal on the emissions trading scheme also “makes sense” as having the UK and the EU both “in the European energy market also offers up opportunities for both sides”.

Martin was perhaps the only leader offering any sort of detailed answer on the EU-UK relations when asked about the hold-up caused by the lack of agreement on tuition fees, with most of them just delivering general platitudes about the EU-UK relationship post Brexit.

Czech Republic’s Andrej Babiš chuckled and said he thought it was a mistake for Britain to leave, but welcomed its involvement in peace talks on Ukraine, while Latvia’s Andris Kulbergs said he wasn’t across the detail on that issue.
Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson also said he was “not into details” on that point, but welcomed “a major step forward” in relations with Britain.
There is full coverage of the summit here.
Farage responds to sharp fall in net migration figures - by complaining too many Britons leaving the country

Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, has spent much of his career complaining about there being too much immigration. In response to today’s figures showing it has again fallen (see 9.38am), he is now complaining about – too much emigration by UK nationals! In a post on social media, he says:
double quotation markNet emigration of British people over the last 10 years is nearly 1 million (941,000), we’ve lost a whole generation of young Brits and replaced them with small boat migrants.

Farage is wrong about the numbers. While a large number of people have arrived in the UK on small boats in recent years (217,000 since 2018, when the Home Office started compiling the figures), that is nowhere close to matching the net emigration figure he quotes.
His only social media comment on immigration (so far today) is to say that Reform UK would abolish the graduate visa system. He says:

double quotation markIt’s too hard for young people to get a job in Britain. So Reform will ABOLISH the graduate visa. It lets foreign students stay after their degree for two years, compete for entry-level jobs OR claim asylum! The Tories created it. Labour kept it. I’ll end it.
